d.d: Deviation from moral normality; extreme wickedness, nefariousness, or cruelty.
d.x: Not until the war ended and journalists were able to enter Cambodia did the world really become aware of the enormity of Pol Pot’s oppression.

d.d: A breach of law or morality; a transgression, an act of evil or wickedness.
Extremely large; greatly exceeding the common size, extent, etc.
d.x: The enormous Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System.

d.d: Extremely, greatly: to an enormous degree.
d.x: Gloria is enormously pleased with our progress.

d.d: Used before a noun in the manner of words like some, a bit of, and so on.
d.x: I've already had enough coffee today.
Those pears aren't ripe enough for the children to eat (them).

d.d: Fully; quite; used after adjectives to express slight augmentation of the positive degree, and sometimes equivalent to very.
d.x: He is ready enough to accept the offer.

d.d: Used after certain adverbs to emphasise that a quality is notable, unexpected, etc.
d.x: Talking of Mr Smith, funnily enough, I saw him just the other day.

d.d: A sufficient or adequate number, amount, etc.
d.x: I have enough (of it) to keep me going.

d.d: Stop! Don't do that any more! It is too much!
d.x: I'm sick of you complaining! Enough!
